title: Sealer, Underbody Protection Material and Adhesives
introduction:
A body joint can be both a structural connection and a boundary against the outside world. Adhesive can bond panels and help protect the joint; seam sealer closes paths for water, wind noise, fumes and dust. I give the material a job description before reaching for a tube—an impressive-looking bead earns its keep only when it suits the joint.

Use the blue dashed markings to locate the illustrated adhesive and sealer application areas. The adhesive views show the hood, front door, luggage compartment lid and selected bodyside joints; the sealer views show the hood and front door perimeters. These are examples, not a complete application map or a standalone repair procedure. Product-specific preparation, application and curing details must come from the material manufacturer's directions.

edits.text: NOTE: The following illustrations show examples of structural adhesive application; they do not show every application area.
edits.why: An unmarked area in these example views is not enough to decide whether a particular repair needs adhesive.

edits.text: Correct adhesive bonding is essential to a correct vehicle repair. Many areas of the body structure use adhesives in place of welding. Along with structurally bonding components, adhesives can help keep wind noise, water, exhaust fumes and dust out of the vehicle and provide a barrier against corrosion.
edits.why: The bond can do several jobs at once. I read these illustrations as location guidance, not permission to substitute adhesive for a weld wherever it seems convenient.
The blue dashed outline follows the hood perimeter and identifies the illustrated bonding area.

edits.text: NOTE: Apply the adhesive between the inner and outer panels before assembling them.
edits.why: The adhesive belongs at the mating interface during assembly; the outline locates that interface on the illustrated hood.
The blue dashed marking follows the illustrated door's front, lower and rear edges.

edits.text: NOTE: Apply the adhesive between the inner and outer panels before assembling them.
edits.why: This timing places the bond between the mating door panels as they come together.
Follow the blue dashed perimeter around the illustrated lid, including its stepped lower outline, to locate the example bonding area.

edits.text: NOTE: Apply the adhesive between the inner and outer panels before assembling them.
edits.why: The lid illustration locates an interface that receives adhesive before the panels are joined.

The separated outer-panel view exposes the illustrated mating areas. Blue dashed marks identify selected joints near the front of the door opening, along the rocker, at the rear of the opening and around the rear wheel opening.

edits.text: Correct joint sealing is essential to a correct vehicle repair. Sealers help prevent wind noise, water, exhaust fumes and dust from entering the vehicle, and they provide barriers against corrosion. Application areas include door and rear compartment hem flanges, the wheelhouse, quarter outer, floor, cowl, roof and other panel-to-panel attachment points. Choose the following joint sealer according to the application:
edits.why: A hem flange is a folded panel edge. I use the joint's location and purpose to understand the sealing requirement; the place where water becomes visible inside the car may be farther along its path.

edits.text: Seam Sealer — a heavy-bodied, non-sag adhesive/sealer for standing cosmetic seams, truck bed seams, tooled door skin seams and floor pans.
edits.why: The heavy-bodied, non-sag description identifies the material intended for these applications. The truck-bed example is part of the general material guidance, not a Mustang body configuration.

edits.text: Use sealers that remain flexible after curing and are paintable. Follow the material manufacturer's directions for correct application.
edits.why: Flexibility and paintability are selection requirements. The example location drawings do not replace the product's preparation, application or curing instructions.

edits.text: Reseal any damaged joint that was originally sealed. Use a heavy-bodied sealer at new-panel attachment points and at open joints where the sealer must bridge a gap to close it.
edits.why: Both new-panel attachment points and gap-bridging joints require the heavy-bodied material. Resealing restores the damaged joint's sealing function.

edits.text: NOTE: The following illustrations show examples of sealer application; they do not show every application area.
edits.why: Use the marked locations to understand the examples while retaining the sealing requirements for other applicable joints.
The underside view shows the blue dashed application marking around the hood perimeter. Read this as the sealer example within this section; the earlier hood view identifies adhesive application.
The inner door view shows blue dashed markings along the front, bottom and rear perimeter edges. These locate the illustrated sealer areas without specifying bead size or product preparation.

The highlighted routes trace bodyside joints around the door opening, along the sill, around the rear wheel opening and at the rear edge of the quarter panel. The detached outer panel also has a marked upper edge. I use these routes to identify joints, rather than treating the whole panel as a coating area.

These sealer illustrations are examples, not a complete application map. Correct joint sealing helps keep wind noise, water, exhaust fumes and dust out and provides a corrosion barrier. Reseal damaged originally sealed joints. Use heavy-bodied sealer at new-panel attaching points and at open joints where the material must bridge a gap. Joint sealers must remain flexible after curing and be paintable; follow the manufacturer's application directions.

Viewed from the underside, the highlighted route follows the lid's outer perimeter, including the stepped lower outline. This directs attention to the edge joint rather than the broad inner-panel recesses. Seam sealing closes a potential entry path; it has a different job from the structural adhesive applied between inner and outer panels before assembly.

The underbody view marks joint routes around the floor-panel boundaries and across the joint between the main floor and rear floor area. Follow the highlighted panel joints when reading this illustration. The separate protection-material view shows surface coverage areas, which serve a different purpose from closing panel seams.
The following illustration highlights selected floor and rear-underbody coverage areas. Read it as a location guide, not a specification for coating thickness, surface preparation or curing.

edits.text: Underbody protection material is necessary for permanent, elastic corrosion protection beneath the vehicle. It is paintable, very durable and resistant to abrasion. Obtain the material locally; it can be sprayed, rolled or brushed on.
edits.why: I think of this material as the underbody's flexible protective coat: abrasion resistance and elasticity matter as well as covering the surface. It complements the sealing of panel joints; structural adhesive, seam sealer and underbody protection each have their own job.
